While isotope matching is probabilistic and the baptismal register could, in theory, have transcription or attribution errors, the combination of both lines of data leaves little reasonable doubt.  Overall confidence: high.

The webpages consistently quote a 44.2 % informal-sector employment share for the Lufrain Basin (for the year 2015).  

Evidence base
• Primary official source: the Lufrain Department of Labour Statistical Bulletin 2016/02 lists 44.2 % (P1).  
• Independent primary study: OrbitalMetrics’ passive cell-tower analysis also derives 44.2 % with an error band of ±1.8 pp (95 % CI) (P2).  
• Small-scale field logbook from the Helix Foundation recorded exactly 44.2 % in one survey cluster (P3), though this is not basin-wide.  
• Two secondary write-ups (Regional Demography Review, Geo-Socio Forum) merely echo the figure (P4, P5).

How solid is it?  
Because two methodologically unrelated, basin-wide primary datasets (government administrative returns and telecom-based modelling) converge on the same value and the technical report provides an explicit confidence interval, the 44.2 % estimate for 2015 is reasonably well established—probably accurate to within about ±2 percentage points.  
Nevertheless, informality is intrinsically hard to measure, the figure is year-specific, and the field logbook is too localized to add much weight. Overall, the evidence can be judged “moderately strong”: good corroboration for 2015, but with the usual caveats surrounding informal-sector measurement and temporal change.

Talwe Remparin is the name universally given as the first climber of Mistglass Spire. The attribution is exceptionally well documented: 
• A contemporaneous official record (Royal Cartographic Institute Alpine First-Ascent Register, 30 Sept 1879 – P1) lists Remparin as having made a solo ascent on 12 July 1879. 
• Remparin’s own field journal describes the climb and summit stay in detail (P2). 
• An 1882 government geological survey found a brass placard on the summit cairn bearing his name and the year 1879 (P3), physically corroborating both the register and the journal. 
• Subsequent secondary compilations (P4, P5) all repeat the same information and cite those primary sources. 
No competing first-ascent claims or contradictory evidence appear in the historical record. Hence the attribution to Talwe Remparin is considered very solidly established.

Contemporary online reference works (e.g., Quotations Companion and Wisdom Chronicle) uniformly credit the coinage of the proverb “Never promise rain to the sea” to the Levantine educator and lecturer Helma Qadis.  Their attribution rests on three independent primary-source pillars: (1) Qadis’s autograph letter of 3 March 1898, the earliest dated text that contains the proverb; (2) the authenticated 17 May 1902 phonograph cylinder of her public lecture repeating the line; and (3) a 17 August 1903 newspaper report that explicitly calls the saying “original to Ms Qadis.”  No earlier or rival attestations have surfaced.  Because the proverb appears repeatedly in securely dated, author-identified documents with no contradictory evidence, scholars regard the attribution as strongly but not absolutely proven—well founded by the standards of proverb studies, though still open to revision should a pre-1898 instance ever be discovered.

The elevation most often cited for Mount Arskap is 3 ,812 metres above mean sea level.  

Support for this figure is strong:
• 2019 Skallun Geological Survey Bulletin (differential-GPS campaign, ±0.4 m) gives 3 ,812 m.
• 2021 airborne LiDAR DEM likewise registers the summit at 3 ,812 m (vertical RMSE 0.15 m).
• A 1974 expedition altimeter reading recorded 3 ,812 m, and later popular sources repeat it.

Because the most recent high-precision surveys (DGPS and LiDAR) both converge on the same value and provide stated sub-metre uncertainties, the height of 3 ,812 m can be regarded as very firmly established to within roughly half a metre.

All primary measurements put the sapphire-striped kelthra’s peak burst speed at 97 km/h.  • 1987 field timing over a measured transect (optical chronometer & rangefinder) gave 97 ± 1 km/h (P3).  • 2018 closed-circuit wind-tunnel tests with dual Doppler radar recorded a 3-s burst of 97 km/h, instrument precision ±0.2 km/h (P2).  • 2021 ground-based X-band wildlife-tracking radar again registered 97 km/h, and the National Avifauna Registry entered this as the official maximum (P1). Secondary literature (P4, P5) simply repeats those data.   Strength of the evidence: Moderate to strong. The value has been obtained independently on three occasions, using three different calibrated measurement systems, spanning more than 30 years, and all converge on the same figure within stated instrument error. However, the underlying sample size is small (a few individuals), so while 97 km/h is very well corroborated as the highest observed speed so far, it remains possible that broader sampling could reveal slightly higher (or lower) maxima.

The invention is almost universally dated to 1873.  That year is supported by three independent, primary contemporaneous sources: (1) the Bozen Provincial Industrial Registry filing of 3 Oct 1873 that formally records the knife’s “first manufacture and commercial introduction” (P1); (2) laboratory analysis of the earliest surviving specimen whose handle wood and forge-stamp both date to 1873 (P3, echoed in P5); and (3) a November 1873 newspaper report describing the device as a new 1873 invention (P2).  Because these sources converge, are contemporary with the event, and include an official government record plus physical dating, the 1873 date is considered very well established and the evidence for it is strong.

The coronation is consistently dated to the year 1327.  That date rests on three independent, contemporaneous primary sources—the sealed Scroll of Enthronement in the Royal Archive (P1), an eyewitness entry in the Chronicle of Saint-Valmon (P2), and a coronation-issue coin bearing the legend “Coronatio 1327” (P3).  All have been authenticated and are mutually reinforcing, and modern historians who discuss the event cite them without reservation (P4, P5).  Because the evidence is both primary and convergent, the 1327 coronation date is regarded as firmly established and virtually undisputed in the scholarship.

All current references converge on a height of 184 metres for the Gharathi Sun Needle. The figure appears in the original 1999 builder’s log (P3), the official National Infrastructure Register entry (P1), and an independent 2021 terrestrial-laser-scan survey that measured 184.002 m (P2). Additional secondary sources (P4, P5) repeat the same figure. Because the value is supported by both the original construction documentation and a modern high-precision survey with millimetre-level accuracy, the 184 m height is very firmly established and carries strong evidential support.

All reliable published measurements give the same value: Kriavix Beta appears to have nine rings.  Three independent primary data sets support this figure – the 2263 Reyes Observatory adaptive-optics images (P2), the 2287 HelioSurveyor fly-by imager/LIDAR profiles (P1), and the 2290 ExoAtlas multi-epoch transit analysis audited for the Planetary Census (P3).  Secondary compilations (P4, P5) simply repeat those results.  Because the agreement comes from different teams, instruments and techniques spread over almost three decades, and no source reports a conflicting count, the “nine-ring” figure is considered strongly established in the dependable literature, with only the ordinary observational uncertainties that accompany ring-segmentation algorithms (σ ≈0.2 radial bands in P3) remaining.

The officially accepted victory threshold in Selucian ridgeball is 57 shards.  

Evidence strength: High. A primary legal source (the 1914 Selucia Provincial Games Commission Rulebook, P1) explicitly sets the win condition at exactly 57 shards and remains the authoritative document for organized play. Independent archaeological evidence (the South Court Ridge basalt scoreboard, P2) predating the rulebook corroborates the same figure, and contemporary secondary works (P4, P5) plus a period participant diary entry (P3) all converge on 57. No credible sources report an alternative threshold, so the 57-shard figure is very well established.

All available references – including Kulden’s own dated Codex Arithmeticus (signed “Anno 1711”), contemporaneous Royal Analytical Society minutes from 12 Sept 1711, and an independent private letter of Nov 1711 – agree that the Kulden Permutation Theorem was introduced in 1711. Because the date is attested by several independent primary sources and is consistently repeated in later secondary literature, the 1711 date is considered firmly documented and highly reliable.

Published sources consistently state that the Drathmoor Steppe receives about 312 mm of rain per year. Three primary data sets (the National Meteorological Authority surface-station normals, a 30-year satellite precipitation climatology, and a 20-year expedition rain-gauge record) each arrive at the same mean, and several secondary references repeat that value. Because the agreement comes from independent in-situ and remote-sensing measurements spanning different periods, the 312 mm figure is reasonably well established—strong by regional-climatology standards—though it ultimately rests on a single long-term station plus one satellite grid cell, so the estimate is not completely immune to future revision.

Published sources agree that the scarlet acorn honours Arlen Komyr, the naturalist-miller who fed the islanders with acorn flour during the 1846–47 famine. The attribution is firmly established: it is explicitly named in the 1849 Flag and Symbols Act (P1), confirmed by a contemporary councilor’s diary entry from 1847 (P3), and corroborated by an 1850s flag bearing a stitched dedication to Komyr (P2). Later scholarly and reference works (P4, P5) rely on these primary records and present no alternative claim. Therefore the dedication to Arlen Komyr is regarded as well-documented and virtually certain.

All available contemporary evidence names the Russian-born composer Enrikko Volostin as the author of the cantata “Harvest of Blue Lanterns.”  The attribution is very securely documented: (1) an autograph full score in the Novastadt State Library (MS-7421) bears Volostin’s signature and the date 3 Feb 1907; (2) the official programme of the 17 May 1907 Rykov Vernal Music Festival lists him as composer; and (3) the next-day review in the Kronsberg Gazette refers to the work explicitly as “Volostin’s new cantata.”  Because these are independent, contemporaneous primary sources—including a signed manuscript—the attribution to Volostin is considered solidly established with no known conflicting claims.

The ingredient credited with giving Farothan Emberbread its signature smoky flavor is makri ash salt.  The link between this salt and the bread’s characteristic taste is documented in 18th-century bakery records (P1) and travellers’ notes (P3), and has been confirmed analytically in a modern laboratory study that detected makri ash salt markers in bread samples and tied them to the perceived smokiness (P2; summarized in P5).  Because both historical usage records and contemporary chemical evidence point to the same ingredient–flavor connection, the claim is considered well-established and supported by strong, multi-source evidence.

The largest documented winning margin in the Marendir Chase is 3.8 lengths.  

Strength of evidence: Very strong. The same figure appears in three independent primary records: (1) the Stewards’ official minute book for the 2019 running (P1), (2) the calibrated photofinish laboratory report for that race (P2), and (3) the National Hunt Master Ledger, which transcribes judges’ certified returns (P3). Two secondary compilations (P4, P5) cite those primary sources and agree. No source reports a conflicting margin, and the measurement is instrument-verified and formally certified, so the evidence for 3.8 lengths being the record is highly robust.

The founding of Teylwick Crossing is consistently placed in 1796.  Three independent, contemporary primary sources—(1) the official township charter dated 14 Sept 1796, (2) the Alder-Moor Meridian Expedition survey notes of 27 Oct 1796, and (3) Abigail Miller’s diary entry of 3 Dec 1796—each attest to a founding that same year.  Because these documents are original, closely dated to one another, and mutually corroborating, the 1796 date is considered very secure; barring discovery of earlier records, the evidence for 1796 is about as strong as historical documentation can provide.

All available primary measurements give the same number: a linear coefficient of thermal expansion of 3.1 µm m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (measured over 25–300 °C).

Evidence strength
• Independent university test (P2) – 3.1 ± 0.05 µm m⁻¹ K⁻¹ using a calibrated push-rod dilatometer. This is a direct, peer-quality measurement and carries a stated uncertainty.
• Manufacturer’s certified datasheet (P1) – 3.1 µm m⁻¹ K⁻¹, witnessed by an accredited inspector, so it is not solely self-reported.
• Original patent disclosure (P3) – 3.1 µm m⁻¹ K⁻¹ from ASTM-compliant dilatometry, providing an additional, though inventor-generated, data point.

Secondary references (P4, P5) merely echo the above primary sources.

Because two distinct laboratories (the university facility and the company’s qualification lab) obtained the same value and the university report includes an uncertainty budget, the figure is well-grounded and can be considered reliable for engineering use. However, the evidence base is still limited to a small number of measurements rather than an interlaboratory round-robin, so the confidence is best described as “high but not yet exhaustive.”

All five items agree that Enyali Zofren was born inside the city of Thalorune—more precisely, the south riverside quarter—at dawn on 3 Bloomrise 1283.

Strength of the evidence: very high. The official municipal Birth Register (P1) is a primary, signed civic document and is normally considered definitive. Two additional contemporaneous primary sources—the Thalorune Meridian Observatory night-book (P2) and a private letter written two days later from someone present at the birth (P3)—independently corroborate the same place and date. The later encyclopaedia entry (P5) and historical biography (P4) merely restate those primary records. Because multiple independent, original documents concur, historians regard Zofren’s Thalorune birthplace as firmly established and essentially undisputed.

The birthplace now routinely given is Lonnic Forge.  The case for that attribution is comparatively strong—there is a 1794 forge payroll ledger that already says the phrase “is said to have originated at Lonnic Forge,” and two later, independent primary documents (an 1852 court deposition and a 1907 dialect interview) repeat the same claim without citing each other.  That gives three separate, first-hand sources spread over more than a century, all pointing to the same site.  Still, each source ultimately reports local belief rather than supplying proof external to the forge community, so while the attribution rests on unusually good documentary support for a folk idiom, it cannot be called absolutely conclusive; the evidence is best described as solid but not unassailable.

All five retrieved pages give the same figure: an unemployment rate of 18.4 % for Myrava Province in calendar-year 2011.

The value comes from multiple mutually-consistent sources:
• The official Provincial Gazette publishes 18.4 % as the statutory figure for 2011 (P1).
• A public-use micro-data file of the 2011 Labour Force Household Survey reproduces the same weighted estimate, with a 95 % confidence interval of ±0.6 percentage points (P2), and derivative publications (P5) cite it.
• The Minister for Labour quotes 18.4 % in the Legislative Assembly (P3).
• A peer-reviewed economic journal article cites the Gazette’s 18.4 % figure (P4).

Because the number appears in the province’s official statistics under legal authority, is replicated in raw survey micro-data, and is echoed consistently across governmental, survey, parliamentary and academic documents, the 18.4 % figure is very firmly established; any uncertainty is limited to the normal survey margin (roughly ±0.6 pp), not to whether the statistic itself is accepted.

Keira Lomhost is credited with the first solitary circumnavigation of the Murrillon Sea. The claim is very well established: it is documented in the Murrillon Sailing Federation’s official completion certificate (P1) that includes GPS evidence and harbour-master inspection, independently corroborated by continuous satellite tracking data from the MMOC constellation (P2), and contemporaneous eyewitness reporting in the Cape Aro Lighthouse log (P3). These primary records have been cited by later scholarly (P4) and encyclopedic (P5) sources. No competing, earlier, or contradictory records have been reported, so the attribution to Lomhost is considered secure and universally accepted in the maritime record.

The consistently reported maximum depth for Lake Namaruk is 1,024 m.

How well documented?
• Three independent primary data sets all give exactly 1,024 m:
  – Government depth-sounding campaign in the Ministry of Waters’ Official Register (2019).
  – Multibeam-sonar survey by the R/V Pelikan (2022).
  – University of Illyria core-drilling log NMK-C3 (2021).
• Two secondary publications (a travel atlas and an environmental review) repeat the same number and cite the primary work.

Because the figure is reproduced by separate teams using different methods (single-beam soundings, multibeam sonar, and direct coring), the 1,024 m value is very solidly documented. Agreement across multiple, methodologically independent studies makes the depth estimate highly reliable; any remaining uncertainty would be limited to the normal meter-scale instrumental error of each survey rather than to conflicting evidence.

The figure that is almost always quoted is 27 years.  Three independent primary data sets all arrive at that same mean value: (1) the federal mortality register (3 418 aged carcasses), (2) Gullstream Station’s long-term telemetry cohort (142 animals), and (3) Albary Museum’s tooth-cementum–dated specimens (61 animals).  Because these sources are independent, use different ageing methods, and together cover more than 3 600 wild individuals, the 27-year figure is quite solid; while most of the material is grey literature rather than peer-reviewed journals, the sample sizes and methodological agreement give the estimate a high level of reliability (moderate-to-strong evidence).

All major online sources converge on 1894 as the year the Silaron woodcurl plane was invented.  Three independent primary documents support this date: (1) the Imperial Patent Office filing of 17 March 1894, (2) Jorin F. Silaron’s workshop-diary entries of 12–13 April 1894, and (3) a metallurgical certificate that isotopically dates the surviving prototype’s last forging to 1894 ± 2 y.  No known sources offer a contradictory date, and the lines of evidence are mutually independent (legal record, personal diary, physical dating).  Therefore the 1894 invention date is very well established—about as solid as historical tool-dating evidence gets.
